reviewer: Claude Code (AI assistant). Not an independent human review.
method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1779, and of 1778 where they reach the 1779 pages (long-running ones included), every item in 3 or more papers counted again by its opening against every page, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for short items the families miss, phrase searches on all 1,660 pages of 1779 in both transcriptions for every chosen item, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, the others chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: Congress and its paper money, January 1779: the resolutions of 2 January and Congress's address of 13 January
new_groups.definition: Two acts of the Continental Congress on its bills of credit, printed in January and February 1779, often together: the resolutions of 2 January calling on the states for their quotas and taking two emissions out of circulation, and Congress's address of 13 January explaining why it had issued paper money and why it now called for taxes.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress, 2 January 1779: 'Whereas these United States, unprovided with revenues ... have ... been under the necessity of emitting bills of credit': the states' quotas, and two emissions taken out of circulation
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolutions of the Continental Congress of 2 January 1779, headed 'In Congress, January 2, 1779': 'Whereas these United States, unprovided with revenues, and not heretofore in a condition to raise them, have, in the course of the present war, repeatedly been under the necessity of emitting bills of credit, for the redemption of which the faith of these United States has been solemnly pledged...' The resolutions call on the states to raise by taxes their quotas of fifteen millions of dollars for 1779, and, 'whereas many counterfeits have appeared in circulation' of the emissions of 20 May 1777 and 11 April 1778, take those two emissions out of circulation. The Pennsylvania Packet printed them in five issues; four papers print them again after Congress's address of 13 January, which recommends 'the annexed resolutions'. Congress's own resolutions.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Congress, 13 January 1779: 'We cannot review the progress of the revolution which has given freedom to America': Congress's address on its paper money
new_groups.definition: Printings of Congress's address headed 'In Congress, January 13, 1779': 'We cannot review the progress of the revolution which has given freedom to America, without admiring the goodness and gratefully acknowledging the interposition of Divine Providence...' It says that taxation was impracticable at the start of the war, that Congress 'from necessity, embraced the expedient of emitting paper money on the faith of the United States', and that the enemy had counterfeited the bills, and it recommends the resolutions of 2 January to the legislatures. Congress's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Sunbury, Georgia, 25 November 1778: Lieutenant Colonel Fuser's summons to the fort, and Colonel McIntosh's answer, 'Come and take it'
new_groups.definition: Printings of two letters, as the papers published them in January and February 1779 with other papers from Georgia: 'In the morning of the 24th of November Colonel John M'Intosh, commanding officer in Fort Morris, received the following from Lieut. Col. Fuser, commanding a body of British troops, who had the night before taken possession of the upper end of the town of Sunbury': 'You cannot be ignorant that four armies are in motion to reduce this province... if you deliver me the fort which you command, lay down your arms, and remain neuter until the fate of America is determined, you shall, as well as all the inhabitants of this parish, remain in the peaceable possession of your property'; and the answer: 'We, Sir, are fighting the battle of America, and therefore disdain to remain neuter till its fate is determined.—As to surrendering the fort, receive this laconic reply.—Come and take it.' A British officer's summons and an American officer's answer, in an American publication.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The King's speech at the opening of Parliament, 26 November 1778: 'I have called you together in a conjuncture which demands your most serious attention'
new_groups.definition: Printings of George III's speech to both Houses of Parliament at the opening of the session on 26 November 1778, as the papers took it from London papers ('From the London General Advertiser and Morning Intelligencer of November 27, 1778'): 'My Lords and Gentlemen, I have called you together in a conjuncture which demands your most serious attention. In the time of profound peace, without pretence of provocation or colour of complaint, the Court of France hath not forbore to disturb the public tranquillity, in violation of the faith of treaties and the general rights of Sovereigns, at first by the clandestine supply of arms and other aid to my revolted subjects in North-America...' Printed by all seven newspapers that survive for its weeks; admitted by the rule's first part. The King's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Washington's proclamation of 10 March 1779: 'full pardon to all those who shall rejoin their respective corps by the first of May next'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a proclamation 'By His Excellency George Washington, Esq. General and Commander in Chief of the Forces of the United States of America': 'Whereas it hath been represented, that many of those soldiers who have been induced from divers motives to desert their corps, and are now dispersed in different parts of these States, having seen their error, would be glad to return to their duty, but are restrained by the fear of punishment... I do hereby proclaim full pardon to all those who shall rejoin their respective corps by the first of May next', with a warning to those who do not. Given at Head-Quarters, Middlebrook, 10 March 1779. The Pennsylvania Packet printed it in four issues. The commander in chief's own proclamation.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Putnam's account of the enemy's incursion to Horseneck, Camp at Reading, 2 March 1779, sent to Congress by General Washington
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of Major General Putnam's letter dated Camp at Reading, 2 March 1779: 'A detachment from the enemy at Kingsbridge, consisting of the 17th, 44th and 57th British regiments, one of Hessian, and two of new levies, marched from their lines for Horseneck on the evening of the 25th ult. with an intention of surprising the troops at that place and destroying the salt works...' Three papers print it with General Washington's letter to the President of Congress from Head-Quarters, Middlebrook ('I herewith transmit your Excellency an extract of a letter from Major General Putnam, containing an account of the incursion of the enemy to Horseneck'), published by order of Congress; the Virginia Gazette prints the extract alone. Counted by the letter all four print (C-02). An American general's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Charlestown, 3 March 1779: 'Col. Campbell's expedition from Savannah to Augusta ... has proved as unfortunate as Major Gardiner's to Port Royal'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of Charlestown (South Carolina) news dated 3 March 1779: 'Col. Campbell's expedition from Savannah to Augusta, with the Highlanders and Col. Brown's rangers, has proved as unfortunate as Major Gardiner's to Port Royal; to escape a Burgoyne he has made a very sudden and precipitate retreat down the country, leaving us in possession of all the back counties of Georgia, and his friends the Tories to fall a sacrifice, a whole regiment whereof... have already been defeated, and upwards of 150 of them made prisoners.' new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Governor Livingston of New Jersey to Sir Henry Clinton, Elizabeth-Town, 15 April 1779: 'I received your Excellency's letter of the 10th instant this afternoon'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter from William Livingston, Governor of New Jersey, to the British commander in chief, Sir Henry Clinton, answering Clinton's letter of 10 April, which a New York paper had published with Livingston's letter of 29 March: 'I received your Excellency's letter of the 10th instant this afternoon, and had an opportunity about an hour thereafter, to see a copy of it in the New-York American Gazette, together with mine of the 29th of March, which occasioned it...' The New-York Gazette, printed in the city the British held, prints it under its own introduction, which calls the writer 'titular Governor of that province'. new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Thomson Mason to the President of Congress, Leesburg, 17 May 1779: 'about forty sail of the enemy appeared in Hampton Road'
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Thomson Mason to the President of Congress, dated Leesburg, Virginia, 17 May 1779: 'My son, who is immediately from Hampton, informs me, that about forty sail of the enemy appeared in Hampton Road on Sunday the 9th instant. On Monday they attacked our fort at Portsmouth, where Major Matthews commanded with 150 men...' It goes on with the fort given up, ships burned on the stocks, and a party intercepted at the Great Bridge. The New-Hampshire Gazette of 8 June prints another letter of Mr. Mason's of the same day, in other words, sent on by General Gates; it is not counted with this one. new_groups.label: Philadelphia, 25 May 1779: a general meeting of the citizens at the State-House Yard, General Roberdeau's address, and the meeting's resolutions on prices
new_groups.definition: Printings of the proceedings of a general meeting 'of the Citizens of Philadelphia, and Parts adjacent, at the State-House Yard in this City' (held on 25 May 1779): 'General Roberdeau was unanimously requested to take the Chair, who introduced the Business with the following Address: Gentlemen, Although I feel pain from the situation in which you have been pleased to place me, it is with pleasure I meet you, my Fellow Citizens, to consider and determine upon measures for our mutual and public happiness...' new_groups.label: Congress to the inhabitants of the United States, 26 May 1779: 'The present situation of public affairs demands your most serious attention'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of Congress 'To the inhabitants of the United States of America', done in Congress by unanimous consent on 26 May 1779 and signed by John Jay, President: 'Friends and Countrymen, The present situation of public affairs demands your most serious attention, and particularly the great and encreasing depreciation of your currency requires the immediate, strenuous, and united efforts of all true friends to their country...' new_groups.label: Philadelphia, May 1779: 'The last advices from South Carolina inform that the British army had entered that State, with intent ... to get possession of Charlestown'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of news dated Philadelphia, 27 May 1779 in some papers: 'The last advices from South-Carolina inform that the British army had entered that State, with intent, it was supposed, to get possession of Charlestown, and that Count Pulaski has had a smart skirmish, in which his horse was killed under him with fourteen balls... but as General Moultrie was in their front, and General Lincoln in their rear, both with a considerable army, it was very probable there would be another Burgoyneade.' new_groups.label: Commodore Sir George Collier and Major General Tryon, July 1779: their address to the inhabitants of Connecticut
new_groups.definition: Printings of the address of the commanders of a British expedition to the Connecticut coast in July 1779: 'By Commodore Sir George Collier, Commander in Chief of His Majesty's Ships and Vessels in North-America; and Major-General William Tryon, Commanding His Majesty's Land Forces on a Separate Expedition. Address to the Inhabitants of Connecticut. The ungenerous and wanton Insurrection against the Sovereignty of Great-Britain, into which this Colony has been deluded by the Artifices of desperate and designing Men for private Purposes...' It is dated on board the Camilla in the Sound, 4 July 1779. The Newport Gazette, printed in the town the British held, prints it on 8 July (a separate sheet of that paper, which the collection files under 2 July although it prints the address and a Newport paragraph of 5 July, is left out until its date is settled); the Connecticut Courant prints it as one of 'the following insolent Addresses' left in New Haven by the British troops, and the Pennsylvania Packet and the New-Jersey Gazette after General Parsons's letter on the expedition. Satirical verses printed under the same title by three papers are not counted. The British commanders' own address.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1779 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: South Carolina, 22 June 1779: 'General Lincoln having received such intelligence of the intention, strength, and position of the enemy, as rendered it advisable to attack them at Stono Ferry'

new_groups.label: The King of Spain's manifesto, delivered in London by his ambassador the Marquis d'Almodovar, June 1779: 'All the world has been witness to the noble impartiality of the King'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the paper the Spanish ambassador delivered in London in June 1779 before leaving, which Lord North laid before the House of Commons as 'a true translation of the manifesto delivered by the Spanish Ambassador': 'Spanish Manifesto. All the world has been witness to the noble impartiality of the King, in the midst of the disputes of the court of London with its American colonies and with France...' It sets out Spain's grievances and ends that the King 'finds himself under the disagreeable necessity of making use of all the means which the Almighty has intrusted him with'. Most papers print it from an English paper brought to Salem from Bilbao; the New-York Gazette prints another translation ('The world can bear witness to the noble partiality of the King') within the House of Lords' proceedings, and the Pennsylvania Packet prints it a second time within the King of Spain's own decree from the Madrid Gazette of 29 June ('All the world has been witness to my noble impartiality'). Counted together (C-02). The Spanish court's own declaration, in English translations.

new_groups.label: Boston, August 1779: 'arrived here the Continental frigates Providence, Queen of France and Ranger', with ships of a Jamaica fleet

Some papers print 'Sunday last', and the Connecticut Courant 'Saturday se'nnight' (a week before); the papers differ on how many of the prizes had arrived and where. A Boston paper's report.

new_groups.label: The King's proclamation of 9 July 1779: 'Whereas we have received intelligence that preparations are making by our enemies to invade this our kingdom'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a proclamation of George III given at St. James's on 9 July 1779, as the papers took it from London papers: 'Whereas we have received intelligence that preparations are making by our enemies to invade this our kingdom... and to the intent that they may not, in case of their landing, strengthen themselves by seizing the horses, oxen and cattle of our subjects...' It charges the officers of the coasts to have the cattle and provisions driven inland 'upon the first approach of the enemy'. The King's own proclamation.

new_groups.label: Congress, 28 September 1779: John Jay appointed minister plenipotentiary to Spain, Samuel Huntington chosen President, and the thanks of 1 October to Mr. Jay
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of the journals of Congress: 'In Congress, Sept. 28, 1779. Congress having appointed the Hon. John Jay, Esq; their Minister Plenipotentiary, to negotiate a treaty of amity and commerce and of alliance between the United States of America and his Catholic Majesty, and he having signified his acceptance of that office, and thereupon resigned the chair, Resolved, That Congress proceed to the choice of a President...'; Samuel Huntington was elected, and on 1 October Congress thanked Mr. Jay for his conduct in the chair. Congress's own journal.

new_groups.label: General Lincoln to Congress, Charlestown, 22 October 1779: 'In my last of the 5th ultimo, I had the honor of informing Congress that Count d'Estaing was arrived off Savannah'
new_groups.definition: Printings of Major General Lincoln's letter to the President of Congress, Charlestown, 22 October 1779, published by order of Congress: 'In my last of the 5th ultimo, I had the honor of informing Congress that Count D'Estaing was arrived off Savannah: Orders were immediately given for assembling the troops...' It goes on through the march, the siege and the assault, and ends by referring Congress to the officer who carries it. The New-York Gazette, printed in the city the British held, prints it under its own heading: 'Lincoln's Letter to the Congress. Acknowledging the Defeat of the French and Rebels, in Georgia.' An American general's own report.

new_groups.label: General Gates to the President of Congress, Newport, 27 October 1779: 'this Island was evacuated by the enemy's troops on the night of the 25th instant'
new_groups.definition: Printings of extracts of Major General Gates's letter to the President of Congress, dated Newport, 27 October 1779: 'I have the honour to acquaint your Excellency, that this Island was evacuated by the enemy's troops on the night of the 25th instant, and the next morning the army under my command took possession of the town of Newport; I have further the pleasure to inform your Excellency, that the enemy did not commit any wanton destruction upon their leaving the Island...' An American general's own report.

new_groups.label: Congress, 17 November 1779: the public audience of the Chevalier de la Luzerne, minister plenipotentiary of France, with his address and the President's answer
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia report of Congress's entertainment and public audience for the new French minister: 'Last Wednesday an entertainment was given by Congress to the Minister Plenipotentiary of France, at which were present by invitation several Foreigners of distinction, and gentlemen of public character. In Congress, November 17, 1779. According to order the Hon. the Chevalier De la Luzerne, Minister Plenipotentiary of his Most Christian Majesty, was introduced to an audience...', with the minister's address ('Since treaties dictated by moderation have fixed upon a permanent base the Union of France with the American Republic...') and the President's answer. The minister's and Congress's own words, in a Philadelphia report.

new_groups.label: Congress, 19 November 1779: 'Whereas the fluctuating state of prices not only causes inequality and injustice in private dealings': laws to limit prices recommended to the states
new_groups.definition: Printings of the resolutions of Congress of 19 November 1779: 'Whereas the fluctuating state of prices not only causes inequality and injustice in private dealings, and in furnishing the public supplies from the several States, but renders it impracticable to make the proper estimates for future expences, and to fix equitable salaries...' They recommend that the states pass laws limiting the prices of labour and of articles of domestic produce, 'not to exceed twenty fold of the prices current through the various seasons of the year 1774', from 1 February 1780. Two papers print them with the President's letter sending them to the states; the Pennsylvania Packet printed them twice. Congress's own resolutions.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1779 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 625 items printed somewhere; by the finder's count 4 reach 7 papers, 11 reach 6, 60 reach 5 and 156 reach 4). The same script was run with year 1778 over the 1779 pages (items_from_1778.json: 16 items, none in more than 3 papers). Every finder item in 3 or more papers (496) was counted again by its own opening against every page of 1779 in both transcriptions: first by about 100 words, then, because a short item's 100 words take in the paragraph printed after it, by the first 40 words (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams). Items read from different printings of one text were merged, and the parts of one document joined (a letter with the enclosures printed with it, a day's resolutions of Congress under one heading, an address printed in parts). A sweep of the year for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers, as the 1803 review introduced (X-1803-09), found short items the reuse families had not joined; each was counted by its own opening. The 30 chosen items were then counted by their openings with phrase searches over all 1,660 pages of 1779 in both transcriptions, and every hit was read.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, about as many stories as a standard year (about 20 to 35, a target, not a quota); digests are not admitted. One item of 1779 is printed by every surviving paper: the King's speech of 26 November 1778 (7 of 7). From the other eligible items 29 were chosen, in 26 stories (two parents with five groups), covering every month and the kinds of news of the year (the war in America; Congress, the currency and public life; Britain, Spain and the war at sea). Where several items of one affair reach the bar in the same weeks, the most widely printed is chosen and the others are listed as not chosen, unless they are separate public acts (X-1800-01): General Washington's two letters on Stony Point and the thanks of Congress are three public acts. Nothing is held back for its subject.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1779 has 9 catalogue series, which are 9 papers: no paper is under two catalogue numbers. The Pennsylvania Packet (Philadelphia, three a week), the New-York Gazette, and the Weekly Mercury (New York, held by the British; Mondays), the Connecticut Courant (Hartford; Tuesdays), the New-Jersey Gazette (Trenton; Wednesdays) and the New-Hampshire Gazette (Portsmouth; Tuesdays) run all year; the Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) from 12 February; the Newport Gazette (Newport, held by the British) on 25 March and from 1 July to 6 October; the New-Jersey Journal (Chatham) and the Gazette of the State of South-Carolina (Charlestown) have one issue each (16 February, 15 September). Papers in print in any three weeks: 5 in January, 6 or 7 from February to July, 7 or 8 in August and September, 6 from October; the bar is 4 papers almost all year and 5 where an item's weeks hold both the Newport Gazette and the South Carolina issue. Every count here counts eligible pages of issues the release dates to 1779.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: By the first 40 words of their openings, the eligible items are as listed in not_admitted (with their counts); one item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks (the King's speech of 26 November 1778, 7 of 7). The chosen items were counted by phrase searches and every hit read; their counts and the papers that survive for their weeks are in the README's table of stories.
counted_item_by_item.Joins made by the finder: The finder chains items printed together: Congress's resolutions of 2 January with its address of 13 January and the resolutions of 14 January; the papers from Georgia (General Prevost's proclamation, Colonel White's postscript, Colonel Fuser's summons and the answer); General Moultrie's and General Putnam's letters; General Washington's letters on Stony Point, General Wayne's report, the returns and the thanks of Congress; runs of London, Charlestown and Boston news. Each text was counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.Printed forms counted together: C-02: the King of Spain's manifesto in two translations, and once within his own decree from the Madrid Gazette (7 papers); General Putnam's letter printed inside General Washington's letter (3 papers) or alone (1); the account of the attack at Stono Ferry under two headings (an officer's letter, 4; 'authentic intelligence received by his Excellency the Governor', 1).
counted_item_by_item.Printed again counts again: C-08: the Pennsylvania Packet printed Congress's resolutions of 2 January in five issues, General Washington's proclamation in four, and the Charlestown report of Colonel Campbell's retreat and Congress's resolutions on prices twice each; the Pennsylvania Packet printed the Spanish manifesto in two forms a week apart.
counted_item_by_item.Pages that only quote, and texts that sh: C-07 and C-06: a page that quotes an item's first sentence inside other text is not counted (the Pennsylvania Packet's meeting resolutions of 3 July quoting Congress's address of 26 May); an extract that leaves out the opening is not counted (the Virginia Gazette's extract of Congress's circular letter of 13 September, which is then in 3 papers and below the bar); different texts that describe the same men in the same words are counted apart (the three texts on Lieutenant Governor Hamilton, each below the bar).
counted_item_by_item.A sweep for short items: As in the 1803 review (X-1803-09), every page of 1779 was swept for passages shared word for word (seven-word sequences) by 4 or more papers: of 1,538 shared passages, 1,458 lie within the finder's items, 9 are advertisement formulas, and the other 71 were read; the items they hold were counted by their own openings (none of them is chosen).
counted_item_by_item.This year's printings: C-11: the King's speech of 26 November 1778, Colonel Fuser's summons of 25 November 1778 and Congress's resolutions of 19 November 1779 are counted by their printings of 1779.

for_user_decision.The choice under the amended rule (B1): As built: 27 stories (25 single stories, and 2 parent stories with 5 sub-stories), 161 printings in all 9 papers; one story admitted by the rule's first part (the King's speech), 29 items chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news, and the other eligible items listed as not chosen with their counts. for_user_decision.The single issues of the New-Jersey Jour: As built: each counts among the papers that survive for an item's weeks, as the rule reads. The South Carolina issue of 15 September raises the bar to 5 papers for items whose weeks hold it and the Newport Gazette, and it keeps the King of Spain's manifesto (7 of 8) and the Charlestown paragraph (7 of 8) from being printed by every surviving paper; the New-Jersey Journal's issue of 16 February does the same for Congress's resolutions of 2 January (6 of 7).
for_user_decision.Printed forms counted together: As built (C-02): the King of Spain's manifesto in two translations and within his decree (7 papers; the English translation alone, 6); General Putnam's letter with or without General Washington's covering letter (4; with the letter, 3); the Stono Ferry account under two headings (5; as the officer's letter, 4).
for_user_decision.Both sides: As built (R-02): the British commanders' address to the inhabitants of Connecticut, Colonel Fuser's summons, and the reprints of the New-York Gazette, printed in the city the British held, with its own headings and introductions (Governor Livingston, 'titular Governor'; 'Lincoln's Letter to the Congress. Acknowledging the Defeat of the French and Rebels, in Georgia'), are described by whose account they are, in the papers' words.
for_user_decision.General Sullivan's expedition: As built (R-02): the letter from an officer in General Sullivan's army is admitted as that officer's account of the burning of the towns of the Six Nations; its description says that it is not the Six Nations' account.
for_user_decision.A ship lost with her crew: As built (R-04): the Boston report of a brig wrecked in a gale off Plymouth in December 1778, and of her crew's sufferings (4 of the 5 papers that survive for its weeks), turns on private persons and is not admitted without your decision; it is listed under 'for the owner' without names.
